KEY MESSAGE 1...Light rain continues this afternoon into early 
Monday morning. Breezy, cloudy, and cooler Monday afternoon.

A raw, cool, and rainy afternoon continues across southern New 
England, with rain persisting through much of the evening. 
Rainfall will be predominantly stratiform with generally light 
to occasionally moderate rainfall rates. A rumble of thunder 
cannot be ruled out near the south coast, though the risk is 
quite low. Overall, additional rainfall amounts of 0.25-0.75 
inch are expected, with some localized variability. Flooding is 
not a concern with this event. Rain gradually shifts offshore 
overnight, coming to an end by or before daybreak Monday. It 
remains raw and wet overnight, with lows in the upper 40s to 
lower 50s and a breezy northerly wind.

As for Monday, showers linger just offshore along a frontal 
boundary while 1030 mb high pressure builds in from the 
northwest. This results in a tightening pressure gradient and 
breezy north-northeast winds throughout the day, especially near
the coast where gusts top out around 20-25 mph. Clouds hang 
tough for much of the day, though there may be a few glimmers of
sunshine. It will remain cool, with highs ranging through the 
60s. Clouds remain Monday night as well, with lows falling into 
the 40s across much of the region, while the urban centers 
remain in the lower 50s.

KEY MESSAGE 2...Dry and cool through mid week. Watching the 
potential for a coastal low to form mid to late week, bringing 
chances for strong winds and rainfall heading into the weekend.

Ensemble guidance remains in good agreement that an anomolously
strong high pressure system will develop over Quebec Tuesday 
and linger into Wed/Thurs. This system likely keeps temperatures
across New England cooler than normal, in the low to mid 60s, 
with a cooler airmass and several days of prolonged 
northeasterly flow. Despite the large areal coverage the 
Canadian high spans, guidance indicates the formation of a weak 
Tuesday across the Mid-Atlantic region that could push just far 
enough north into NJ to brush southern New England with spotty 
showers. Still some uncertainty in how far north that low could 
move, but general consensus in some low-end PoPs across the 
southern coast Tuesday... higher chances across southern CT, 
closer to NYC.

Both deterministic and ensemble guidance continue to indicate 
potential for a coastal low to form Wednesday into the later 
half of the week. While there is still a large amount of 
uncertainty in the forecast this time, the overarching trend has
been the low slowly meanders north into the waters south of 
Nantucket; however, each model has this low taking a slightly 
different track: the GFS pushing further NE and closer to 
Nantucket, and the ECMWF further NW and closer to Long Island. 
Regardless, this system is likely to bring strong winds, rain, 
and the potential for erosion/coastal flooding.

Highest confidence at this time pertains to winds, especially 
over the waters. As the low deepens and approaches to the south,
the Canadian high over Quebec is also likely to strengthen and 
expand, leading to a tighter pressure gradient over New England.
Given there's still uncertainty in how strong the low and high 
get as well as the track of the low, there is still some 
question as to how strong the gradient will get. However, 
confidence is increasing in the potential for Gale Force winds 
across the southern waters, and a Gale Watch has been issued for
Tuesday evening through at least Thursday morning. The latest 
ensemble guidance is also showing roughly 50 percent 
probabilities of Storm Force wind gusts across the ocean waters 
south of Long Island and Block Island as well as 20 to 30 
percent probabilities of Storm Force gusts over Nantucket Sound 
and Cape Cod Bay as the low deepens Friday into Saturday. Winds 
over land along the south coast, Cape, and Islands throughout 
the week are more likely to be a touch slower than the marine 
winds, but still gusty... more on the order of 25-35 mph.
